Axholme
AKS-hohm
n. (the Lincolnshire charterhouse of 1397 on the Isle of Axholme, later the scene of the fen drainage riots)
From the town of Haxey with Old Norse holmr, an island in a marsh.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The charterhouse of the Visitation of St Mary was founded in 1397 at Low Melwood on the Isle of Axholme, an area of raised ground amid the Lincolnshire fens. Its prior Augustine Webster was executed at Tyburn in 1535 with the priors of Beauvale and London. In the 1620s Cornelius Vermuyden drained Hatfield Chase and the surrounding levels under a grant from the crown, and the commoners of Axholme, whose rights of pasture and turbary went with the water, rioted, broke the works and litigated for decades. This dictionary records Axholme for that long quarrel over boundaries, because the removal of a landmark is one of the few property offences Scripture names repeatedly and curses. The command is blunt, “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark” (Deu 19:14). Solomon repeats it twice, “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28), “Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless” (Pro 23:10). Job lists it among the works of the wicked, “Some remove the landmarks; they violently take away flocks, and feed thereof” (Job 24:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land; a boundary as a limit; a common as land held in common by a community; to encroach as to enter on the rights of another; and drainage as the act of draining land.

expand to see more

LANDMARK, n. Any mark or fixed object; as a marked tree, a stone, a ditch, or a heap of stones, by which the limits of a farm or other portion of land are designated.

BOUNDARY, n. A limit; a bound; that which marks the extent of a possession or a territory.

COMMON, n. An open ground, or that soil the use of which belongs equally to the inhabitants of a town or of a lordship.

ENCROACH, v.i. To enter on the rights and possessions of another; to intrude; to take possession of what belongs to another, by gradual advances.

DRAIN, v.t. To filter; to cause to pass through some porous substance; to empty by drawing off gradually, as a marsh.

Key Scripture

Deu 19:14 — "Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance, which thou shalt inherit in the land that the LORD thy God giveth thee to possess it."

Pro 22:28 — "Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set."

Pro 23:10 — "Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless:"

Job 24:2 — "Some remove the landmarks; they violently take away flocks, and feed thereof."

Modern Corruption

Lincolnshire charterhouse of 1397 on a fen island: its prior died at Tyburn, and its commoners spent decades fighting the drainage of their commons.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how seriously Scripture treats a boundary. A landmark was a stone in a field, and moving it at night transferred land without anybody appearing to steal anything, which is exactly why the law names it, “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set” (Deu 19:14). Solomon repeats the command and attaches it, the second time, to the defenceless, “and enter not into the fields of the fatherless” (Pro 23:10).

The second thing is the company such an act keeps in Scripture. Job lists the moving of landmarks in the same breath as driving off flocks and oppressing the poor, as the ordinary business of men who prosper by it, “Some remove the landmarks; they violently take away flocks, and feed thereof” (Job 24:2). The drainage of Hatfield Chase was good engineering and enriched a crown and a contractor by extinguishing the rights of people who had no deeds; a village that rioted for sixty years had read its Proverbs, “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gebul (H1366), a boundary; Hebrew cug (H5253), to remove; Hebrew yathom (H3490), the fatherless; Hebrew gazal (H1497), to take by violence; Hebrew 'olam (H5769), of old time.

expand to see more

Hebrew gebul (H1366) — a border, a landmark; “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark”, Deuteronomy 19:14.

Hebrew 'olam (H5769) — of old, long established; “which they of old time have set”, Deuteronomy 19:14.

Hebrew cug (H5253) — to move back, to displace; “Remove not the ancient landmark”, Proverbs 22:28.

Hebrew yathom (H3490) — the fatherless, without a deed; “and enter not into the fields of the fatherless”, Proverbs 23:10.

Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to seize, to take by force; “they violently take away flocks”, Job 24:2.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark” (Deu 19:14) — theft that leaves no thief visible."

"“and enter not into the fields of the fatherless” (Pro 23:10) — attached, the second time, to the defenceless."

"“Some remove the landmarks” (Job 24:2) — the company the act keeps."
